Proposed Revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC of the MISO Tariff in Response to Show

Dear Secretary Reese: 
 
 
Pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”),1 Part 35 of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) regulations,2 and the Commission’s 
directives in the Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act 
(“Show Cause Order”),3 the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., (“MISO” as the 
Transmission Provider),4 on behalf of American Transmission Company LLC, by its corporate 
manager, ATC Management Inc. (collectively, “ATC”)5, hereby submits proposed revisions to 
Attachment FF-ATCLLC of MISO’s Open Access Transmission, Energy, and Operating Reserve 
Markets Tariff (“Tariff”).   
Paragraph 36 of the Show Cause Order indicates that Transmission Owners may elect to 
submit their own FPA Section 205 filings to address matters discussed in the Show Cause Order.  
Because ATC currently has its own local planning process included in Attachment FF-ATCLLC 
of the MISO Tariff, ATC is proposing certain revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC to fulfill 
obligations outlined in the Show Cause Order to address large load integration in the ATC 
service territory.  ATC understands that MISO intends to file various amendments to its Tariff in 
future filings to comply with the Commission’s directives in the Show Cause Order and ATC

footprint and be complementary to MISO’s future filings.  As described below, ATC’s proposed 
revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC describe processes that are designed to work together with 
MISO’s process in the same way ATC’s local planning process in Attachment FF-ATCLLC 
works with the annual MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) process today.  ATC also 
seeks approval for modifications to the local planning process that is utilized today in ATC’s 
footprint.   
I. 
Background 
A. 
ATC 
ATC is a Wisconsin limited liability company created as a single-purpose, for-profit 
transmission company.7  ATC began operations under the terms of its own open access 
transmission tariff on January 1, 2001, and currently owns and operates over 10,000 miles of 
jurisdictional transmission facilities in the states of Wisconsin, Illinois, Minnesota, and 
Michigan.  Many of ATC's facilities were acquired, with Commission approval, from a number 
of previously vertically integrated companies, municipalities, and electric cooperatives.  On 
February 1, 2002, ATC transferred operational control of its facilities to MISO.8  Since that time, 
MISO has provided transmission service over ATC’s transmission facilities pursuant to the terms 
of the MISO Tariff, with ATC operating its transmission facilities at MISO’s direction.  ATC has 
its own Commission-approved local planning process set forth in the MISO Tariff at Attachment 
FF-ATCLLC. 
B. 
ATC’s Planning Functions and Attachment FF-ATCLLC 
Since beginning operations in 2001, ATC has engaged in local transmission planning as 
one of its core functions.  ATC’s local transmission planning process is open, collaborative, 
driven by stakeholder needs, and responsive to industry changes and technology developments.  
Attachment FF-ATCLLC sets forth ATC’s planning functions and the manner in which ATC 
meets the transmission needs of its customers, which is a key element of ATC’s operations.  
Pursuant to Wisconsin law,9 ATC is a transmission only company and not permitted to directly

serve retail customers.  Therefore, ATC engages in the necessary planning to provide for 
changes, modifications, or additions to its transmission facilities to provide adequate, reliable, 
and sufficient transmission capability so that entities that rely on ATC’s transmission facilities 
are able to meet the needs of their respective retail customers.   
ATC’s planning processes are structured to include all interested parties and treat all 
similarly situated interconnected customers in a similar, consistent manner.  Additionally, while 
ATC maintains its own planning processes in Attachment FF-ATCLLC, ATC coordinates 
extensively with MISO.  Under the Transmission Owners Agreement,10 ATC conducts “bottom-
up” local planning to implement its planning functions and obligations to ensure the adequacy 
and reliability of the ATC system for the benefit of all customers.  As the utility industry changes 
and new technology develops, especially with the recent advent of large load data centers, ATC 
has actively engaged with the changing landscape to continue to fulfill its obligations.   
C. 
ATC’s Distribution – Transmission Interconnection Process   
Attachment FF-ATCLLC sets forth ATC’s process for Distribution – Transmission 
Interconnections.  The process is initiated by one or more of ATC’s distribution customers 
through submission of a Load Interconnection Request Form (“LIRF”).  Upon receipt of a 
complete LIRF, ATC will begin its studies and analyses of the interconnection.  More 
specifically, ATC will engage with its Best Value Planning process, as defined in Attachment 
FF-ATCLLC, and collaborate with the customer to determine the best value solution to 
interconnect the new load request.   
 
Upon ATC’s development of the project containing the transmission facilities necessary 
to facilitate the load interconnection in a safe, reliable, and cost-effective manner, ATC 
coordinates with MISO and engages with MISO’s planning process.  ATC will submit the 
proposed project to MISO either through the annual MTEP process or MISO’s Expedited Project 
Review (“EPR”) process.  Upon MISO’s approval, the project would be included in Appendix A 
of MTEP.   
 
As an active participant in the MISO stakeholder process, ATC is aware that MISO is 
developing proposals to comply with the requirements in the Show Cause Order.  ATC will 
continue to engage with the stakeholder process and work with MISO to ensure that ATC’s local 
planning and interconnection processes in Attachment FF-ATCLLC comply with the Show 
Cause Order and can be implemented in a manner that complements MISO’s process.  ATC 
intends for the revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC to integrate into MISO’s processes in the

same way ATC’s existing Distribution – Transmission Interconnection process interplays with

D. 
ATC’s Development of Large Load Studies and Requirements  
In 2022, ATC began receiving serious inquiries about potential new large loads, and in 
particular data centers.  While ATC had already developed a robust local planning process, 
internal planning experts quickly realized that more than traditional steady state analysis would 
be needed to appropriately study and determine the system impacts of the unique characteristics 
presented by large load data centers.  ATC began intensive internal studies and engaged with 
vendors to develop concepts for mitigation of key concerns related to large data center loads.  
Subsequently, in 2024 through 2025, ATC elevated its engagement with external 
resources, including specialized power system consultants.  Specifically, ATC and its consultants 
engaged with new and unique types of analyses to study large loads, including flicker analysis, 
rotor swing modes, and generator shaft studies.  ATC determined that to safely and reliably 
interconnect large loads, more robust planning criteria requirements that apply specifically to 
these new, unique large loads must be developed and implemented.  Development of these 
requirements posed unique challenges as there was no industry documentation of these issues, 
concerns, impact, mitigation measures, or performance requirements.  Authorities such as NERC 
had not yet engaged with these issues.  Recognizing the need for transformation in response to 
the characteristics of new large loads, ATC stepped into the role of industry leader in developing 
reliability criteria.  
Each new large load presents its own unique characteristics and challenges, however 
ATC realized early in the development phase that it would not be practical to perform custom 
studies for each load interconnection request and to derive bespoke project-specific limits to 
address reliability concerns.  Therefore, through intensive studies and analyses, internally and 
with consultants, ATC developed new local planning criteria, including new criteria developed 
exclusively to apply to large load interconnections across ATC’s footprint.  Uniquely situated 
among the Great Lakes and Mississippi River, ATC’s geography stands out from other areas in 
the MISO footprint.  Additionally, as a transmission-only company, ATC has developed close 
relationships with its customers.  These factors have contributed to ATC’s ability to develop 
processes and requirements that are specifically applicable to ATC’s system without 
compromising reliability.  
Through studies and analysis, ATC initially determined that the appropriate threshold for 
categorizing large loads in the ATC footprint would be 200 MW.  As discussed below, ATC 
continues to analyze, on no less than an annual basis, the appropriate threshold for categorizing 
large loads and associated reliability and operational criteria.  Through the proposed Attachment 
FF-ATCLLC updates described below, ATC is now updating its large load threshold to 100 MW 
to align with directives from the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin (“PSCW”) regarding 
appropriate measures to mitigate cost shifting concerns at the retail level.11  ATC has determined 
 
11 See Public Service Commission of Wisconsin Order Docket 6630-TE-113 Final Decision (PSC REF# 591873) 
(“PSCW Retail Tariff Order").  The PSCW made a finding of fact that it would be “reasonable to make the VLC

that 100 MW is an initially appropriate threshold for categorizing large loads for cost allocation 
and to ensure reliability, but will continue to re-evaluate and apply reliability criteria for large 
loads that present unique characteristics as necessary.  ATC also continues to be an active 
stakeholder and participant in MISO and NERC efforts to ensure reliable service.  ATC will 
continue to be responsive to industry standards, as needed.   
As described in depth below, ATC proposes to revise Attachment FF-ATCLLC to 
include requirements, processes, and procedures associated with the interconnection of large 
loads, including the operational and reliability requirements discussed above.  
II. 
Discussion  
ATC’s proposed revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC are just and reasonable.  The 
Commission acknowledged in the Show Cause Order that ATC has its own distribution 
interconnection request process and load interconnection procedures described in Attachment 
FF-ATCLLC, but that Attachment FF-ATCLLC did not explicitly address interconnections of 
large loads.12  Over the last few years, ATC has developed company-specific business practices 
containing policies, practices, and requirements directed specifically at large loads that also 
address several concerns identified by the Commission in the Show Cause Order.13  Therefore, in 
this filing, ATC is seeking to amend Attachment FF-ATCLLC to add these requirements and 
processes associated with large loads in ATC’s footprint.  
 
As discussed above, many of the revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC reflect existing 
processes, practices, and requirements in ATC’s footprint.  Therefore, ATC’s proposed revisions 
should not disrupt existing commercial arrangements and in-flight projects.  By allowing ATC to 
maintain existing process and requirements, while seamlessly building in additional requirements 
and provisions necessary to address several of the Commission’s concerns in the Show Cause 
Order, the proposed revisions are just and reasonable and will provide clarity and transparency 
for the reliable interconnection of large loads in the ATC footprint.14

A. 
Interconnection Process for Large Loads 
1. 
Application Process  
i. FERC Directive 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary finding that the MISO 
Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks an application process for Eligible 
Customers15 seeking transmission service on behalf of large loads.16  The Commission 
emphasized that “clear and consistent provisions” will deter speculative requests and provides 
certainty and clarity for stakeholders.17  The Commission indicated that applications should be 
accepted on a rolling basis.18 
ii. ATC Compliance  
As the Commission acknowledged in the Show Cause Order, ATC has developed local 
planning processes and requirements in Attachment FF-ATCLLC, including processes for 
Distribution – Transmission Interconnections.19  ATC’s local planning process for Distribution – 
Transmission Interconnection applies to all ATC customers (i.e., Eligible Customers), including 
large loads, seeking transmission service on ATC’s system.   
ATC proposes to add the following Tariff language to further clarify that the Distribution 
– Transmission Interconnection planning functions, processes, and requirements apply to large 
loads:  
• Sections V.C and VI.A.1 state that Distribution – Transmission Interconnection 
Planning Function includes Large Load Distribution – Transmission 
Interconnection Planning.  
 
15 Defined by MISO as “(i) Any electric utility (including the Transmission Owner(s), ITC Participants(s), and any 
power marketer), Market Participant, Federal Power Marketing Agency, or any person generating electric Energy 
for sale or resale is an Eligible Customer…; or (ii) Any retail customer taking unbundled transmission service 
pursuant to a state requirement that a Transmission Owner or ITC Participant offer the transmission service, or 
pursuant to a voluntary offer of such service by a Transmission Owner or ITC Participant, that is an Eligible 
Customer under this Tariff.  Unbundled retail customers that seek to take local distribution service cannot be 
Eligible Customers under this Tariff with respect to that service.”  MISO, FERC Elec. Tariff, Module A, §1.E 
(Definitions E) (93.0.0).  In ATC’s footprint, an Eligible Customer includes ATC’s distribution customers with 
which ATC has a Commission-accepted Distribution – Transmission Interconnection Agreement.  Any new 
distribution customer in ATC’s footprint would be required to enter into a Distribution – Transmission 
Interconnection Agreement prior to interconnecting to ATC system to ensure compliance with ATC’s requirements 
and procedures as outlined in Attachment FF-ATCLLC.

The Distribution – Transmission Interconnection process in Attachment FF-ATCLLC 
details clear and specific procedures for submitting a load interconnection request form 
(“LIRF”), which kicks off applicable study procedures as described below.  ATC accepts 
applications on a first-come, first-served basis, upon completion of applicable readiness 
requirements, also described below.  ATC proposes additional Tariff language to Attachment FF-
ATCLLC to establish these procedures, including:  
• Section IV defines the LIRF as the form in which a distribution customer initiates 
a request for a distribution interconnection to ATC’s system that includes a 
request for service to a large load.  
• Section IV also includes in the definition of “Distribution – Transmission 
Interconnection Requests” that the processes for distribution interconnections in 
ATC’s footprints apply to large load interconnections, plus any requirements or 
processes exclusively applicable to large loads. 
• Section VI.A.1-2 provides clarifying edits to sections of Attachment FF-ATCLLC 
addressing Distribution – Transmission Interconnection Requests and Study 
Sequencing to establish procedures that apply to large load interconnections. 
Generally, ATC’s established local planning procedures in Attachment FF-ATCLLC 
apply to large load interconnections, as clarified by the proposed revisions above.  Notably, 
however, certain existing and proposed new requirements will apply exclusively to large loads.  
These large load-specific requirements are detailed herein.  ATC has added the following Tariff 
language to state that while the general Distribution – Transmission Interconnection Process 
applies to all loads in ATC’s footprint, including large loads, certain requirements apply 
exclusively to large loads:  
• Section III proposes to add to the “Purpose” section of Attachment FF-ATCLLC 
Tariff language stating that ATC has developed certain policies that apply 
exclusively to large loads. 
Importantly, as described above, ATC’s application process and studies of all distribution 
interconnections, including large load interconnections, contemplates close coordination with 
MISO.  While ATC has developed its own process to accept and study distribution 
interconnections within its footprint, ATC works closely with MISO to provide it with all 
necessary information so that the interconnection can be integrated into the annual MTEP, which 
may include on an as needed basis, review and approval on an expedited timeline through 
MISO’s Expedited Project Review (“EPR”) process.  Upon Commission acceptance of these 
changes to Attachment FF-ATCLLC, ATC will continue to coordinate with MISO to ensure all 
projects interconnecting to ATC’s system are included in MTEP either through the standard 
planning process or the EPR process.  
2. 
Readiness Requirements  
i. FERC Directive

August 17, 2026

The Commission indicated that sufficient readiness requirements may be necessary to 
address concerns associated with speculative large loads.20  The readiness requirements may 
include a fee and certain requirements associated at different phases of the study process.21  
Further, as a component of the readiness requirements, the Commission indicated that it may be 
helpful to collect information regarding the characteristics of the large load customer.22 
ii. ATC Compliance  
Prior to initiation of a System Impact Study (described in detail below), ATC requires all 
distribution customers to meet certain readiness requirements to deter speculative requests and 
ensure accurate studies.  First, distribution customers must submit a LIRF that is deemed 
complete, pursuant to criteria outlined by the applicable ATC Business Practice.  Additionally, 
any distribution customer that seeks to add a new large load must submit a Large Load 
Interconnection Criteria Confirmation Form which details specific operating characteristics of 
the proposed load increase so that ATC has sufficient information to appropriately analyze the 
large load impacts.  Other documentation may be necessary prior to ATC’s initiation of the 
System Impact Study to ensure that ATC can accurately study the new interconnection and 
ensure resources are allocated only to non-speculative requests.  ATC proposes to add these 
requirements to Attachment FF-ATCLLC, including:.  
• Section VI.A.4 contains a new section detailing the readiness requirements to 
initiate a System Impact Study, including requirements specifically applicable to 
large load interconnections.   
Additionally, ATC proposes to implement a new requirement associated with large load 
interconnections in response to the Commission’s Show Cause Order.  Any new distribution 
interconnection request that exceeds the large load threshold shall be required to pay an initial 
non-refundable deposit, in an amount of $50,000 which will be established by the applicable 
ATC Business Practice.  Subsequently, the distribution customer shall be invoiced by ATC for 
time and materials above and beyond the initial deposit necessary to complete the System Impact 
Study.  In ATC’s experience, implementation of this charge will help to defer speculative 
requests and ensure that distribution customers will provide accurate and up to date information 
to ATC when submitting a new LIRF and other required documentation.  
• Section VI.A.5 adds a section requiring an initial deposit and any time and 
materials cost in exceedance of the deposit necessary for ATC to complete the 
System Impact Study.

3. 
Study Procedures  
i. FERC Directive  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission expressed concern that the MISO Tariff 
lacked specific study procedures for Eligible Customers seeking transmission service on behalf 
of large loads for new and incremental additions.23  Additionally, the Commission indicated that 
studies to produce a non-binding good-faith estimate of the cost and time to construct facilities 
necessary to interconnect a large load customer should take no more than 90 days to complete.24  
The Commission also indicated that studies should consider operational characteristics and that 
accurate models using Electromagnetic Transient studies may be helpful in analysis of large 
loads.25 
ii. ATC Compliance  
As described above, Attachment FF-ATCLLC has guided ATC’s interconnection process 
since its adoption in MISO’s Tariff.  In response to the Commission's Show Cause Order and 
changing industry needs, ATC proposes to add additional detail and requirements to its 
distribution interconnection study process.  Upon completion of all applicable readiness 
requirements as discussed above, ATC will initiate a System Impact Study.  System Impact 
Studies are split into two distinct phases:  (1) steady state analysis, and (2) applicable special 
studies.   
All load interconnections require ATC to conduct the steady state analysis.  The steady 
state analysis phase of the System Impact Study shall result in a non-binding good-faith estimate 
of time, cost, and potential facilities necessary to interconnect a load, responsive to the 
Commission's directives outlined in the Show Cause Order.  Upon completion of the steady state 
analysis, ATC can move into the special studies phase, as needed.  Not all load interconnection 
requests require special studies, and the extent to which depends upon the complexity of the 
project.  However, potential projects that exceed ATC’s large load threshold or display unique 
characteristics will require additional studies during the special studies phase.  The special 
studies phase includes analysis of, but is not limited to, transfer analysis, reactive power analysis, 
angular and voltage stability of nearby generators, load voltage stability, voltage ride through of 
both generators and loads, power quality analysis, short-circuit analysis, and other transient study 
analyses.  The special studies phase analyses may also involve several positive sequence and 
Electromagnetic Transient study tools and result in technical reports or recommendations for 
potential mitigation of any limitations observed. 
ATC proposes to include the requirements of System Impact Studies in Attachment FF-
ATCLLC and include additional detail, procedures, or other relevant information associated with

4. 
Evaluation of Alternative Transmission Technologies  
i. FERC Directive  
 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission expressed concern with the lack of clear and 
consistent provisions requiring the evaluation of alternative transmission technologies.26  The 
Commission indicated that transparent and clear requirements for the evaluation of these 
technologies be included in Tariff language.27  Similarly, the Commission indicated that a study 
report should indicate why alternative transmission technologies are not feasible in the event no 
alternative transmission technology facility is used in response to a request to interconnect a 
large load.28  
ii. ATC Compliance  
Attachment FF-ATCLLC requires ATC to engage in Best Value Planning, which is 
defined as: 
[T]he consideration of, or evaluation of, one or more alternatives to the proposed 
construction of new, or the modification of existing, Transmission Facilities 
which have been identified in a planning process to determine whether an 
alternative or alternatives exist that may include the construction of new, or the 
modification of the existing, Distribution Facilities or Transmission Facilities 
owned by others that is/are less costly or which may provide greater enhancement 
to the reliability, capability or integrity of ATCLLC’s Transmission Facilities and 
such interconnected Transmission or Distribution Facilities when compared to the 
estimated cost of the construction and capability of the proposed new, or the 
proposed modification of, ATCLLC’s Transmission Facilities, while taking into 
account the environmental considerations, regulatory approvals and the ability to 
construct the proposed Distribution or Transmission Facilities in a timely and 
appropriate manner.29

Enhancing Technologies (“GETs ”).  The terms are used interchangeably in ATC’s footprint and may include static 
synchronous compensators, static VAR compensator, advanced power flow control devices, transmission switching, 
synchronous condensers, voltage source converter, advanced conductors, tower lifting, and dynamic line ratings,

To facilitate Best Value Planning, ATC engages with evaluation of grid enhancing 
technologies or alternative transmission technologies for all distribution interconnection requests.  
ATC proposes to make this requirement clear in Attachment FF-ATCLLC through addition of 
new, specific language:  
• Section VI.A.9 adds language detailing that in Best Value Planning ATC shall 
evaluate the use of grid enhancing technologies or alternative transmission 
technologies in each System Impact Study.  
Additionally, Section VI.A.9 requires ATC to provide results of studies to the distribution 
customer, which is commonly referred to as Best Value Planning documentation or reporting in 
ATC’s footprint.  Specific Best Value Planning documentation requirements are detailed in 
applicable ATC Business Practices.  This documentation, which is required by Attachment FF-
ATCLLC, inherently includes narrative information regarding the use of and evaluation of 
alternative transmission technologies.  In the Best Value Planning documentation, ATC provides 
details on the evaluation including, if applicable, details as to why grid enhancing technologies 
or alternative transmission technologies were not used.  
B. 
Large Load Definition and Operational Requirements  
1. 
Large Load Definition  
i. FERC Directive  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission expressed concern due to the lack of a 
definition of large load in MISO’s Tariff that sufficiently captures loads that present unique 
challenges described in the Show Cause Order.30 
ii. ATC Compliance  
As stated above, ATC previously established a threshold of 200 MW to define large loads 
in its system.  To address the Commission’s concerns in the Show Cause Order, ATC is 
proposing amended language in Attachment FF-ATCLLC, Section IV to change the threshold to 
100 MW.  The 100 MW threshold shall serve as ATC’s initial threshold to classify loads to 
which certain requirements, procedures, and processes shall apply to address reliability, 
operational, and cost shifting concerns.  This threshold shall serve as a baseline threshold and 
may be adjusted in appliable ATC Business Practices and local planning criteria as necessary.  
As described above, ATC has determined that 100 MW is an appropriate threshold from 
a planning, reliability, and operational perspective within ATC’s footprint.  ATC consistently 
coordinates with MISO, other regional and national entities, its customers, and other 
interconnected entities to ensure that any process or requirement in ATC’s footprint shall not 
compromise reliability within ATC’s territory, MISO’s service area, or broader.  Additionally, 
the PSCW has recently established that 100 MW is an appropriate threshold to address retail cost 
 
30 Show Cause Order at P 57.

August 17, 2026 
Page 12 
 
 
shifting concerns associated with large loads.31  In its final decisions in a recent retail tariff 
proceeding and recent individual retail contract proceeding, the PSCW determined that it was 
most reasonable to set the applicability threshold at 100 MW.32  The PSCW found that the rates 
and rules established by retail tariffs and retail contracts are appropriately applied to large loads 
greater than 100 MW.33 In an effort to align with the state’s authority over retail rates of ATC’s 
distribution customers, ATC has applied the 100 MW threshold to address cost shifting concerns 
at the wholesale level, as discussed in detail below.   
• Section IV adds a definition of “ATCLLC Large Load” to establish that in ATC’s 
footprint, an initial threshold of 100 MW shall apply. 
2. 
Operational Requirements  
i. FERC Directive  
The Commission expressed concern in the Show Cause Order that the MISO Tariff lacks 
ongoing operational requirements to address the unique characteristics and challenges of large 
loads.34  Specifically, the Commission highlighted several areas of concern, including:  (1) lack 
of sufficient visibility and channels for communication of data; (2) lack of required monitoring 
equipment to monitor impacts such as ramp rate; (3) requirements related to disconnection of 
large loads when necessary; (4) lack of ramp rate or ride-through requirements; and (5) lack of 
necessary protection systems or control technology requirements.35   
ii. ATC Compliance  
As discussed above, ATC has already developed requirements that are applicable to loads

Cost Shifting  
1. 
Agreement to Address Cost Shifting Concerns  
i. FERC Directive  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission expressed concern regarding cost shifting that 
may occur among transmission customers as a result of the interconnection of large loads.37  The 
Commission made a preliminary finding that a pro forma cost recovery agreement between 
MISO, the Transmission Owner, and the Eligible Customer taking transmission service on behalf 
of the large load would mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers.38  
Specifically, the Commission directed MISO and/or the Transmission Owners to address 
situations in which the proposed load fails to materialize or fails to materialize to the extent 
initially anticipated.39  
The Commission references previously filed agreements designed to address such 
concerns, including Transmission Security Agreements as possible ways to alleviate cost shifting

the Transmission Owners to develop methods, processes, and cost recovery agreements by which 
it will provide protections against cost shifting.41  The Commission also made a preliminary 
finding that any such cost recovery agreement should require credit support and/or security 
sufficient to secure obligations of customer taking transmission service to paid the amounts 
owned pursuant to the agreement.42 
ii. ATC Compliance  
For the past two years, ATC has engaged with its customers and other stakeholders to 
address the concerns described by the Commission.  Ultimately, this led ATC to develop a new 
Business Practice on Large Load Cost Allocation and develop two new agreements to ensure 
cost shifting concerns are addressed in ATC’s footprint at the wholesale level, and in a manner 
that allows ATC’s customers who provide retail service, are able to comply with directives from 
state authorities on cost shifting prevention at the retail level.  Specifically, ATC has developed a 
Large Load Project Commitment Agreement (“LLPCA”) and a Minimum Transmission Charge 
Agreement (“MTCA”) that it will enter into with its distribution customer.  Pursuant to ATC’s 
Large Load Cost Allocation Business Practice, ATC requires these agreements if the project 
exceeds the definition of large load (i.e., 100 MW), or exceeds $100M in costs.  The PSCW has 
determined that 100 MW would be an appropriate threshold in the State of Wisconsin to 
adequately protect against cost shifting concerns.43  Further, ATC recognized the need to address 
the potential impact from new loads that may be smaller than 100 MW, but because they are in 
areas of the system that have less transmission buildout than others, drive a disproportionate 
amount of network upgrades.  Therefore,  ATC intends to ensure that no cost shifting occurs for 
distribution interconnection projects that drive projects that exceed $100M in cost.  
ATC recently filed several LLPCAs and an MTCA associated with a large load in its 
footprint44 and intends to develop additional LLPCAs and MTCAs with in-flight projects in its 
footprint.  The protections provided by the LLPCA and MTCA work in tandem, each described 
in detail below.  
The LLPCA is designed to protect the Parties and other wholesale customers from costs 
associated with construction of facilities tied to a new large load and in the event of project 
cancellation, termination, or substantial modification prior to the project being placed in service.    
Likewise, ATC can invoke the terms of the LLPCA in the event of cancellation, termination, or 
substantial modification to recoup costs incurred during project development and construction.

cost shifting during project development and construction.   
After ATC’s transmission facilities go into service, the MTCA provides additional 
protections to prevent cost shifting associated with transmission buildout in the event the large 
load that formed the basis for the buildout fails to materialize.  As an initial step pursuant to 
ATC’s Large Load Cost Allocation Business Practice, ATC coordinates with the distribution 
customer pursuant to Attachment FF-ATCLLC through the Best Value Planning process, as 
described above, to develop a proposed project including facilities necessary to adequately serve 
the distribution customer, and by extension, its end-use customer.  The distribution customer will 
continue to benefit from ATC’s entire transmission system and therefore will continue to pay for 
Network service pursuant to the MISO Tariff.  Additionally, under the terms of the MTCA, the 
distribution customer will pay for Network Service for all capacity it has requested, regardless of 
actual use, so that other customers do not bear those costs.  However, the charges incurred under 
the MTCA will be limited to the incremental revenue requirement for the transmission facilities, 
such that the distribution customer, and by extension, its customer, will not subsidize 
transmission service for other customers.  
The protections provided by the LLPCA and MTCA are directly responsive to the 
Commission’s Show Cause Order related to large load interconnections.45  In the Show Cause 
Order, the Commission preliminarily found “that MISO’s Tariff appears to be unjust and 
unreasonable because it lacks adequate mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among 
transmission customers, which may result in unjust and unreasonable rates for transmission 
service.”46  The LLPCA and MTCA provide a mechanism by which ATC’s other wholesale 
customers are protected during the period of construction and also in the event the large load 
end-use customer fails to materialize or fails to take service to the full extent of its request to 
ATC’s distribution customer.  The protection mechanisms provided by the LLPCA and MTCA 
directly respond to the Commission’s concerns on the risk of unjust cost shifts.47  The Amended 
LLPCAs and MTCA offer the protections that the Commission is seeking in a fair, just, and 
reasonable manner and similar to other accepted cost recovery agreements, such as Transmission 
Security Agreements, which the Commission recognizes in its Show Cause Order.48

that just and reasonable cost recovery agreements would require credit support or other financial
